..
Wednesday: A ridge off the Canadian coast will continue to promote a 
drying and warming trend for the Inland Northwest through the rest 
of the day. The early morning contains a chance of fog through the 
northern valleys in eastern Washington and in the Northern Idaho 
Panhandle. Visibilities could drop to a half mile or less, impacting 
the morning commute for people those areas. The ridge will be at its 
strongest today, with the increase in heights bringing a 6-8 degree 
increase in high temperatures across the area. Winds from the south 
will increase over the Columbia Basin, Waterville Plateau, and 
Okanogan Valley, resulting in a breezy evening for these areas with 
wind gusts 15-20 mph. 

Thursday through Friday morning: A low pressure system strengthening 
over Western Canada and then moving into Central Canada will usher a 
trough across the region Thursday afternoon and evening. This will 
bring strong winds, localized blowing dust potential and fire 
weather concerns, and mountain rain to the region. 

Of most impact will be winds increasing ahead of the trough moving 
through the area Thursday morning through evening. For much of the 
Waterville Plateau, Wenatchee, Columbia Basin, Moses Lake, 
Spokane/CdA, and Palouse areas, there is a 60-70 percent chance of 
maximum wind gusts greater than 30 mph. In the Waterville Plateau 
and Columbia Basin, wind gusts up to 40 mph are possible. This will 
result in blowing objects and trouble driving, especially for high 
profile vehicles. 

Another impactful result of these winds could be localized blowing 
dust and fire weather concerns throughout areas that have not seen 
much recent rain and thus have drier soils. For blowing dust, 
greatest chances will be seen throughout the Waterville Plateau and 
Lewiston/Pullman areas. Blowing dust can bring visibilities down to 
a mile or lower, impacting drivers. Hot Dry Windy Index values 
increase throughout the broader Basin area on Thursday due to the 
gusty winds moving through, bringing a chance for elevated fire 
weather concerns. Impacts include rapid fire spread, especially for 
any existing fires. 

Localized rain chances will be seen in the Idaho Panhandle Thursday 
night into Friday morning. There is only a 10 percent chance for 
accumulations to reach 0.1 inches. However, the moisture over the 
area will result in a returning chance for fog in sheltered northern 
valleys on Friday morning.

Friday evening through Sunday: Lower heights will remain over the 
area on Friday as another low spins off the coast of British 
Columbia. Temperatures will decrease nearly ten degrees between 
Thursday and Friday. On Friday night, as the low nudges closer to 
the state of Washington, there is a 10 to 20 percent chance of 
precipitation in Western Okanogan Valley. 

As the center of the low tracks just south of Washington through 
Oregon Saturday into Sunday, chances of precipitation widely 
increase regionwide. Nearly all of the Inland Northwest has a 20 
percent chance and above at seeing 0.10 inches of rain from Saturday 
night into Sunday afternoon. 

Ahead of the main low passage on Saturday morning, winds will again 
increase throughout much of the area as a north-south surface 
pressure gradient strengthens. Wind gusts through the Basin, 
Waterville Plateau, and Okanogan Valley could reach 35-40 mph 
Saturday morning and afternoon. As the low tracks eastward, winds 
begin to increase in the Idaho Panhandle on Saturday night and 
continue to be elevated with gusts 20-25 mph through Sunday morning. 
Ridgetops could see wind gusts up to 35 mph. Impacts with these wind 
gusts include blowing objects and trouble driving, especially for 
high profile vehicles. 

Saturday night into Sunday, chances for isolated thunderstorms 
increases as the low moves through. Areas from Spokane to Wenatchee 
and southward have a 10 to 20 percent chance of thunderstorms. Mid 
to long range models show CAPE values increasing to 200-300 J/kg, 
and steep 3-6km lapse rates. A heavy caveat to these thunderstorm 
chances is that they could change should the track of the low 
pressure change. Even now, many models show the highest chances for 
thunderstorms outside of our forecast area to the south and east, 
but it is worth a mention and something we'll keep an eye on through 
the week since it could create localized impacts.

Monday through Tuesday: By Monday, clusters are divided on where the 
low will be. About 60 percent of clusters have the low far enough 
eastward that higher heights will start moving over the area. This 
will favor a warming and drying trend. 40 percent of clusters have 
the low closer to the region, which would indicate continuing 
chances for cooler and showery conditions. /AS
